Bugonia

Classification: MIXED

Full analysis below
Film · Theatrical March 5, 2026 Analyzed by VirtueVigil Editorial Team 14 min read

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

NOT A WOKE TRAP. Bugonia presents its satirical framework openly from the first act. Jesse Plemons' Teddy is immediately coded as an unhinged conspiracy theorist, and Emma Stone's Michelle is positioned as the sympathetic corporate victim. The film does not hide its engagement with corporate critique, environmental anxiety, or the pathology of conspiratorial thinking. The third-act reveal that Michelle actually is an alien does not reverse the film's ideological framework; rather, it compounds the nihilism. Conservative audiences will identify the satirical targets within the first twenty minutes. The twist is narrative, not ideological.

Overall Perspective

Classification: MIXED

WOKE 20 | TRADITIONAL 17 | Composite +3 WOKE

SPOILER ALERT: This review contains detailed plot analysis and reveals the film's ending, including the twist. Do not read further if you want to experience the film unspoiled.

Bugonia is the rarest thing in contemporary cinema: a film that genuinely refuses to pick a side.

Yorgos Lanthimos' remake of the 2003 South Korean cult film Save the Green Planet! arrives at a cultural moment perfectly calibrated for its themes. In 2025 America, conspiracy thinking has migrated from internet forums into the halls of power. Anti-corporate sentiment spans the political spectrum. Pharmaceutical companies are simultaneously saving lives and destroying them. Trust in institutions is at historic lows. Everyone knows the system is broken. Nobody agrees on who broke it.

Into this environment, Lanthimos drops a story about a beekeeper named Teddy Gatz (Jesse Plemons) who kidnaps the CEO of a pharmaceutical conglomerate named Michelle Fuller (Emma Stone), convinced she is an alien plotting to destroy Earth. Teddy is coded as everything the cultural mainstream despises: a rural, conspiracy-obsessed loner who has constructed an elaborate mythology to explain the suffering in his life. His mother was poisoned by an Auxolith clinical trial. His bees are dying. His community is disintegrating. Instead of directing his rage at systemic failures he can name, he has channeled it into a conviction that aliens called Andromedans are secretly controlling corporate America, killing the bees, and engineering human subservience.

For roughly 90 minutes, Bugonia appears to be a darkly comic indictment of conspiratorial thinking. Teddy is sympathetic but clearly unhinged. He electrocutes Michelle. He covers her in antihistamine cream to block alien distress signals. He shaves her head. He explains his theory about the Andromedans with the dead-eyed conviction of a man who has crossed the line between righteous anger and psychosis. Plemons plays all of this with such layered humanity that you never stop feeling for Teddy even as you recognize he has lost his mind. It is a performance that defies political categorization because Plemons refuses to reduce Teddy to a caricature. Conservative critics at Worth It or Woke compared it to Daniel Day-Lewis. They were not wrong.

Stone, meanwhile, plays Michelle as a woman who is simultaneously a corporate predator and a kidnapping victim. Her performance in the basement sequences is extraordinary: she shifts from terror to calculation to manipulation to something that might be genuine empathy, and you can never quite tell which is real. When she convinces Teddy that a bottle of antifreeze is an Andromedan antidote for his mother, knowing he will kill Sandy by injecting it into her IV, the cruelty is breathtaking. And yet the film has also shown us that Auxolith's clinical trial genuinely poisoned Sandy in the first place. Michelle's real-world corporate crimes are not fictional. The pharmaceutical company did destroy this family. The conspiracy is wrong about the mechanism (aliens) but right about the harm (corporate pharmaceutical negligence).

This is where Bugonia becomes genuinely provocative. The film spends its first two acts mocking conspiracy culture, then its third act validates the conspiracy. Michelle Fuller actually is an alien. She actually is the leader of the Andromedans. She actually does exterminate all human life on Earth in the film's final minutes, popping what appears to be a clear bubble from the vantage point of her mothership, instantly killing every human being on the planet while leaving all other life untouched. The bees return to Teddy's empty apiary. The birds fly. Humanity is gone.

The ending is not played for horror or tragedy. It is played with eerie beauty. Michelle gazes at the newly quiet Earth with something between sorrow and relief. Jerskin Fendrix's Oscar-nominated score swells with an aching, dissonant grandeur that makes extinction sound almost like mercy. This is the moment that defines Bugonia and the moment that makes it nearly impossible to classify ideologically.

The culture war around Bugonia has been fascinatingly confused, and that confusion is the film's point.

From the left, the film has been read as a critique of conspiracy culture and the paranoid right. Teddy is a QAnon-adjacent figure: a rural white man who has replaced material analysis with fantasy, who sees aliens where he should see capitalism, who kidnaps and tortures a woman because he cannot process his grief through rational channels. The Indypendent called the film 'a worthwhile exploration of conspiracies and corporate culture.' Atmos framed it as a climate horror story. The progressive reading sees Teddy as a tragic case study in misdirected rage and Michelle as a complicated corporate villain who, alien or not, represents the real evil of pharmaceutical profiteering.

From the right, the film has been read as something more subversive. Worth It or Woke noted that 'while 99% of the film seems like it is making fun of right-wing conspiracy lunatics, it is not.' The conservative reading emphasizes that Teddy is proven right about everything. Michelle IS an alien. The corporation IS controlled by malignant forces. The bees ARE being destroyed deliberately. The conspiracy IS real. And critically, Plemons' character delivers dialogue that explicitly calls out both left-wing and right-wing ideologies as 'manufactured tools to pollute the minds of the masses.' The film does not align with either camp. It indicts both.

There is a third reading, articulated on Reddit's TrueFilm community and in several academic-adjacent reviews, that the film is 'pretty conservative in its worldview' because it 'ends up being a defense of wealth inequality and a condemnation of taking radical action to end it.' In this reading, Teddy's violence against Michelle is a metaphor for revolutionary action against the ruling class, and the film punishes him for it by making his methods ineffective and his analysis correct but useless. Michelle wins. The system wins. The powerful alien-CEO destroys humanity rather than allowing the conspiracy theorist to expose her. The revolutionary dies. The establishment prevails, even if 'prevailing' means exterminating everyone.

VirtueVigil's assessment: Bugonia is genuinely ideologically ambiguous, and this is neither a dodge nor a compliment. The film contains clear progressive elements: corporate pharmaceutical harm as a central theme, the sympathetic framing of environmental anxiety (colony collapse, climate change subtext), and the portrait of conspiracy thinking as a distorted response to real systemic injustice. It also contains clear traditional elements: the validation of intuition over institutional authority (Teddy was right), the portrayal of corporate elites as literally inhuman, and a nihilistic ending that could be read as a warning about what happens when the ruling class operates without accountability.

The reason the scores are so close (20 Woke, 17 Traditional, +3 margin) is that the film deliberately plays both sides. Every progressive reading is undercut by the twist. Every conservative reading is complicated by Teddy's violence. This is Lanthimos' design. He is not interested in ideological comfort. He is interested in making you squirm.

As a piece of filmmaking, Bugonia is technically superb but structurally flawed. The first two acts are taut, claustrophobic, and brilliantly acted. Plemons and Stone generate the kind of captor-captive chemistry that sustains a two-person drama without a single dull moment. The supporting cast is deployed with precision: Aidan Delbis brings genuine pathos to Don, whose autism is portrayed with sensitivity and whose death (by his own hand, after being promised a trip to space) is the film's most emotionally gutting moment. Stavros Halkias brings unexpected gravitas to the small role of Deputy Casey. Alicia Silverstone's Sandy is mostly unconscious, but her presence haunts the film.

The third act is where opinions divide. Lanthimos' decision to validate the conspiracy and end with human extinction is either a brilliant subversion of audience expectations or a narrative cop-out that undoes the careful character work of the first ninety minutes. The Worth It or Woke review captured this tension precisely: the film 'has the body of a 10 and the soul of a slug.' The ending is intellectually provocative but emotionally unsatisfying. After investing deeply in Teddy and Michelle as complex human characters, the reveal that Michelle was never human at all retroactively cheapens some of that investment.

The score by Jerskin Fendrix deserves its Oscar nomination. Composed without Fendrix ever reading the script, based solely on three words Lanthimos gave him ('Bees, Basement, Spaceship'), it is a work of controlled chaos that mirrors Teddy's psychology with uncanny precision. The discordant orchestral passages during the torture scenes are almost unbearably tense, while the quieter cello passages during Don's scenes add tenderness that the script alone does not quite earn.

Robbie Ryan's cinematography is characteristically excellent. The tight, confined framing of the basement creates genuine claustrophobia, and when the film opens up to the Sarakiniko Beach in Greece for the final scene (Lanthimos wanted the Acropolis but was denied permission), the sudden visual expansiveness hits with the force of a revelation.

Bugonia opened to $1.8 million in its first weekend from 2,043 theaters and ultimately grossed $42.8 million worldwide against a $45-55 million budget. It is a commercial disappointment, continuing the pattern of Lanthimos films that earn critical adulation and awards recognition but struggle at the box office. The film's four Oscar nominations (Best Picture, Best Actress, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Original Score) represent significant Academy validation, but the commercial performance suggests that Lanthimos' brand of provocation has a ceiling with general audiences.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Yorgos Lanthimos

ART-HOUSE LEFT / NIHILIST. Lanthimos is a Greek auteur whose filmography consistently interrogates social conformity, institutional power, and human cruelty. His films are not traditionally progressive in the activist sense, but his worldview is fundamentally skeptical of authority, tradition, and social norms. He is not a culture warrior; he is a provocateur who uses discomfort as a narrative tool. His work in Poor Things (2023) drew fire from conservatives for its explicit sexual content and feminist themes, but The Killing of a Sacred Deer (2017) and Dogtooth (2009) are equally nihilistic toward progressive and traditional worldviews. Lanthimos is not trying to persuade; he is trying to disturb.

Yorgos Lanthimos is a Greek director, screenwriter, and producer. Born in Athens in 1973, he studied film and television at the Stavrakos Film School. His breakthrough feature Dogtooth (2009) was nominated for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film. He followed it with Alps (2011) and The Lobster (2015), which earned a Best Original Screenplay Oscar nomination. The Killing of a Sacred Deer (2017) starred Colin Farrell and Nicole Kidman. The Favourite (2018) earned 10 Oscar nominations and won Best Actress for Olivia Colman. Poor Things (2023) won four Oscars including Best Actress for Emma Stone. Kinds of Kindness (2024) was his most divisive work. Bugonia (2025) is his most expensive production, budgeted at $45-55 million, and his fourth collaboration with Emma Stone. His working method with composer Jerskin Fendrix, where Fendrix composes without reading the script, reflects his broader philosophy of creating through instinct and disorientation rather than conventional narrative logic. He is simultaneously one of the most acclaimed and most polarizing filmmakers working today.

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative adults should see Bugonia with clear eyes. The film will initially feel like a sustained mockery of conspiracy culture, and for its first ninety minutes, it mostly is. But the ending changes everything. Teddy was right. The CEO was an alien. The conspiracy was real. The powerful corporation was controlled by an inhuman entity that ultimately destroys all of humanity with the casual indifference of someone closing a tab on their browser. That is not a progressive ending. It is the darkest possible validation of anti-establishment paranoia. But conservatives should also note what the film does with that validation: nothing useful. Teddy being right does not save him or anyone else. His methods (kidnapping, torture, murder) are condemned by the narrative. His violence against the powerful does not liberate anyone. The conspiracy theorist dies and the alien wins. If there is a message for the right, it is this: being correct about the corruption of elites is meaningless without effective action, and violence is not effective action. Progressive adults will be drawn to the corporate pharmaceutical critique and the portrait of conspiracy thinking as a distorted response to real injustice. They should grapple with the fact that the film ultimately validates the conspiracy and exterminates humanity through the actions of a character coded as a progressive corporate feminist. Michelle's Andromedan monologue about creating humanity, guiding them away from violence, and ultimately giving up is a darkly comic mirror of progressive paternalism: benevolent elites who tried to help the masses, failed, and decided to eliminate them entirely. That is not a flattering portrait of progressive power. The performances are extraordinary. Plemons and Stone are operating at the highest level of their craft. See it for the acting even if the philosophy frustrates you.

Parental Guidance

Rated R for bloody violent content including a suicide, grisly images, and language. A woman is kidnapped, bound, electrocuted, and has her head shaved. A character shoots himself in the head. A man is beaten to death with a shovel. Jars of severed body parts are shown. A man unknowingly kills his comatose mother by injecting antifreeze into her IV. A suicide vest detonation occurs. All human life is exterminated in the final scene. Implied but not graphic sexual content. Strong language throughout. The film's nihilistic worldview and disturbing violence make it inappropriate for viewers under 17. Even mature teenagers may find the combination of graphic violence, psychological manipulation, and species-level extinction deeply unsettling. Adult viewing recommended.
